name: Pedro Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Pedro Abbott, 43, and I operate a drill rig at a large mine. I set up at the marked holes, check the pressure and bit wear, and call for a pause when the ground looks wrong. I'm still new enough that the lead driller checks my setup before we start. My partner works at a school kitchen, and our two children are in school there, which helps with pickup; we have a mortgage and roughly four months of expenses saved from years of careful budgeting. The mine pays a usual operator wage, and there are a few other mines within a drive, but I want to become competent here before trying elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say routine AI can tidy paperwork if the drill crew still checks the ground. I would ask that fault reports stay visible to the person running the rig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My drill shift seems safe in this mild picture, provided the mine keeps its work. Four months of savings helps, but a mortgage makes me careful about unnecessary spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the pressure checklist with the lead driller before each new hole. I'd put the monthly savings transfer on the calendar while both household wages continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly settled about work here. The savings account is not a holiday fund; it is what lets us sleep when the mine closes for maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you used AI on the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then I ask it to explain a term from the drill manual, then confirm the answer with the lead driller. I wouldn't put a machine setting into the rig just because a phone suggested it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I tell them I am learning a trade one careful hole at a time. They know I sometimes come home tired and still check their school notes before bed.

feel: **Calm** about this job path, with sensible concern about the mortgage.

fieldNote: He sees **little job disruption** in the plateau and already follows a careful savings routine.
His occasional AI use stays **informational**; a lead driller checks machine choices and ground conditions.

Continue the monthly savings transfer while both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew planning software might choose holes faster, but the driller must flag unsafe ground. I'd support our union representative asking how drilling targets are set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may lose planners, then each rig may be pushed to drill more holes per shift. I have some savings and other mines nearby, yet a junior driller is easy to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the lead driller to show me one trial of the new plan before changing my setup. I'd take my target records to the union meeting if daily drilling targets rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn a tested plan, but I don't like a target that ignores a cracked bit or wet ground. My worry is that the clock gets the final say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch in a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the proposed hole order with where the crew actually had to stop last week. If the plan misses those delays, I'd put that in writing before using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at another mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if our shifts were cut or the safety pressure became serious. There are a few within driving distance, but I would not move my children for a rumor.

feel: **Anxious** about tighter targets and a junior position, with some options.

fieldNote: His concern is **target pressure** reaching the rig after planning work is automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2028 could replace drilling plans before it can handle the rig itself. I would want a robot timetable for the mine well before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 45 in 2028, I could have only three years before a robot rig threatens my wages. Four months of savings would not cover years of mortgage payments or a long course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the mine's paid drill-maintenance training if a supervised place opens this year. I'd keep my rig shift in 2029 while checking vacancies at the other mines within driving distance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a jolt at the short gap between the two dates. I can learn new equipment, but a trainee wage below our mortgage needs would make the offer useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would training have to pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough to cover the mortgage, food, and the children's school costs without draining our four-month reserve. I'd ask for the wage in writing before putting my name on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a job at another mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply if it still paid a driller and offered supervised work, but robots might reach that mine too. I would not call a longer commute a permanent answer.

I would want a **robot timetable** for the mine well before 2031.

feel: **Alarmed** by the short transition before robot rigs threaten household income.
S2.quote: I would not call a longer commute a permanent answer.
fieldNote: He separates **2028 planning work** from the later robot threat to drilling itself.
Maintenance training needs **written pay terms**; nearby mine vacancies are a possible bridge, not a safe career.

steps.text: Apply for paid drill-maintenance training if a supervised place opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years should buy time for funded apprenticeships, not just more safety posters. I'd ask for workers on the committee that sets robot-rig trials around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 in 2031, and the children would be older with different school bills. A paid mechanical course might give me options, although robots could also change repair work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enroll in a paid mechanical apprenticeship next year if the mine or a nearby employer offers one. I'd save one overtime payment each quarter toward six months of household expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel pressured but not trapped. Five years is enough to start as a beginner again if the training pays and someone teaches me properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2032?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a paid rig or apprentice shift and ask how the robot trial changed actual staffing. I would bring any safety concerns to the union committee with dates and names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your partner increase hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school kitchen has fixed terms and holiday gaps, so I won't build my plan on extra shifts there. Our savings goal would have to come mostly from mine overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children a ten-year warning lets us choose a trade with our eyes open. I'd press the mine to publish training places years before robot rigs arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036, I would probably still need a wage. Our children might be grown by 2039, but I cannot expect their independence to pay our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the local technical college about a paid employer-linked repair course this spring. I'd continue paying down the mortgage principal with half of each annual bonus if one arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the first picture where I could test a new line of work without a rushed leap. I'd still watch whether repair jobs exist after the robots begin servicing themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why look outside the mine for training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A college with local employers could show me actual placements, and several mines are within a drive. I would only enrol if wages or a paid placement keep the household going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do after 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid repair or rig job I had then and compare openings as robots spread toward 2039. If the mine cut my hours, I'd apply to a nearby employer before talking about a house move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The planning work could change at once and a robot rig might reach my shift three years later, before I finish a paid apprenticeship. Written training wages and an honest staffing timetable would help me make a decision for the family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether the training leads to a job at the end. I can take a course. A certificate with no employer attached does not keep the lights on.

headlineQuote: A certificate with no employer attached does not keep the lights on.
portrait: Pedro is a **43-year-old junior** drill-rig operator who asks a lead driller to check setups and unsafe ground.
His partner works in a school kitchen; **four months of savings** and nearby mines offer choices but no permanent shelter.
He uses AI **occasionally** to understand terms and wants to see new planning tools tested on actual holes.
He seeks **paid mechanical training** and real placements, while keeping wages and mortgage costs in view.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** starts a short countdown to robot rigs before he could finish a paid apprenticeship.
whatWouldHelp: **Written training wages** and an honest staffing timetable would let him weigh a course against family bills.
